content: Injuries and wounds are significant public health concerns, requiring both effective therapeutic interventions and robust prevention and control measures. The organization and administration of healthcare delivery systems, including emergency medical services, play a critical role in addressing these issues. Standards for emergency medical services must be established and adhered to in order to ensure optimal outcomes for patients. The World Health Organization (WHO), along with the Department of Violence and Injury Prevention and Disability, and international bodies such as the International Association for Trauma Surgery and Intensive Care (IATSIC) and the International Society of Surgery, have been instrumental in developing guidelines to improve trauma care globally. These guidelines are designed to be universally applicable, regardless of a country's economic status, and aim to define essential trauma care services that should be accessible to all injured individuals. Trauma care systems in high-income countries have demonstrated significant reductions in mortality rates through the implementation of well-organized trauma systems. These systems address all aspects of care, from prehospital settings to initial resuscitation in hospitals and long-term definitive care. However, such systems are minimally implemented in lowand middle-income countries, where over 90% of injury-related deaths occur. To address this disparity, WHO and IATSIC have collaborated to produce guidelines for essential trauma care, outlining the minimum human and physical resources, as well as administrative mechanisms, required to provide effective care. Quality improvement (QI) programs are a cornerstone of trauma care systems in high-income countries and have shown promise in limited applications in lowand middle-income settings. These programs enable healthcare institutions to monitor trauma care services, identify problems, implement corrective measures, and evaluate their effectiveness. By doing so, many preventable deaths can be avoided, and the overall quality of trauma care can be enhanced. Key methods of QI include morbidity and mortality (M&M) conferences and preventable death panel reviews. M&M conferences, when conducted effectively, can identify systemic issues, develop corrective action plans, and evaluate their outcomes. Preventable death panel reviews provide a formal mechanism to assess the preventability of trauma deaths and identify areas for improvement. Both methods are feasible and widely applicable, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced QI techniques, such as the use of audit filters and statistical methods for severity adjustment, provide objective data to monitor and address potential problems in trauma care. These techniques rely on accurate and timely data collection, which may necessitate improvements in medical record systems or the establishment of trauma registries. The guidelines emphasize the importance of adapting QI methods to the realities of lowand middle-income countries while maintaining their effectiveness. They also highlight the need for collaboration among healthcare providers, administrators, and policymakers to strengthen trauma care systems and promote patient safety. In conclusion, these guidelines provide practical, how-to guidance for implementing QI programs in trauma care. They are designed to be applicable to all healthcare institutions, regardless of economic context, and aim to improve the quality of trauma care and save lives. By adopting these methods, healthcare institutions can enhance their existing trauma care activities and contribute to the global effort to reduce the burden of injury-related deaths and disabilities.
